hero.name: Pranay Patil
lines: Engineering taught me how things are built.
Running a business taught me how customers actually behave.
Product management is where both become useful.

decide.title: How I Decide
decide.intro: Five steps. Each links to where I actually used it.

steps.title: Check whether the problem is the problem
steps.body: Problems arrive pre-framed. The first job is finding out whether the framing survives contact with users.
steps.linkText: Uber: the framing said universal, research said concentrated

steps.title: Work out what evidence I actually have
steps.body: Primary, secondary, or my own reasoning. Labelling this honestly changes what I'm allowed to conclude.
steps.linkText: OutLoud: 42 survey responses that didn't match my own target persona

steps.title: Decide, and name what it costs
steps.body: Every choice removes options. The ones worth writing down are the ones where I can say what I gave up.
steps.linkText: Emburse: choosing integration depth over the obvious wedge

steps.title: Build only what serves the core loop
steps.body: Features are cheap to imagine and expensive to maintain. Most of what I cut from OutLoud was cheap to build.
steps.linkText: OutLoud: what I deliberately didn't ship

steps.title: Define the measurement before the result exists
steps.body: Choosing a metric you can't game is harder than hitting one you can.

background.title: Background
background.subtitle: The Short Version
background.intro: How I got here, and what each part taught me.
paragraphs: I trained as an engineer, expecting to spend my time writing code. In 2023, before I graduated, a friend and I co-founded a unisex salon in our area, where none existed yet.

Running the salon gave me a different perspective on building a business. I began paying closer attention to how customers made decisions, how pricing affected demand, and how staffing and day-to-day operations shaped the experience. It was a side of problem-solving I hadn't encountered much in the classroom.

Over time, I realised I enjoyed both the technical side of building things and the process of understanding what people actually need. I wanted to bring those two sides together rather than treat them as separate paths.
Today, the salon runs with just a few hours of my time each week, allowing me to focus on my business analyst role at Ampcus Tech Pvt. Ltd. and projects like OutLoud.

Engineering gave me the technical half. The salon gave me customers and constraints. The analyst work gave me stakeholders and the discipline of writing something someone else has to build from. Product management is where the three stop being separate skills.
